section.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia - Hematologic Parameters and Clinical Signs

sections.section: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) is the most prevalent nutritional deficiency disorder worldwide, arising when systemic iron stores are exhausted and insufficient to support normal erythropoiesis. Clinical manifestations include extreme pallor of conjunctiva and skin, chronic fatigue, generalized weakness, exertional tachycardia, dizziness, cold extremities, brittle nails with koilonychia (spoon nails), angular cheilitis, and pica (unusual cravings for non-nutritive substances such as ice, clay, or chalk). Diagnostic laboratory findings demonstrate microcytic hypochromic red blood cells on peripheral smear, low hemoglobin, reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV < 80 fL), decreased serum ferritin (< 30 ng/mL, or < 100 ng/mL in inflammatory states), and elevated total iron-binding capacity (TIBC).

section.title: Iron Deficiency Anemia - Oral and Intravenous Replacement Therapy

sections.section: Treatment of iron deficiency anemia requires identifying and addressing the underlying source of blood loss (such as gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers or malignancy, or menorrhagia) alongside iron replenishment. First-line therapy is oral elemental iron (100 to 200 mg daily of elemental iron, commonly administered as Ferrous sulfate, Ferrous fumarate, or Ferrous ascorbate). Concomitant administration of ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) enhances intestinal iron absorption, whereas antacids, calcium supplements, tea, and coffee inhibit absorption. Intravenous iron preparations (e.g., Ferric carboxymaltose or Iron sucrose) are indicated in cases of severe malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease on dialysis, or oral iron intolerance.
